items.d: Topical anti-androgen that blocks the hair follicle receptor locally, with minimal absorption into the body.
items.x: A topical anti-androgen that blocks the androgen receptor at the hair follicle, with minimal systemic absorption compared with finasteride. That local action is the appeal — the hair benefit without the sexual side effects finasteride is known for. It has never been through human trials, and development was abandoned decades ago.

items.d: Blocks the NNMT enzyme, which raises cellular NAD+ and shifts fat cells toward burning rather than storing.
items.x: NNMT is the enzyme that breaks down nicotinamide, and fat cells make a lot of it as they expand. Blocking it raises NAD+ inside the cell and pushes fat cells toward burning rather than storing. Most of the interesting work is in cell and animal models, with human data still thin — treat the body-recomposition claims as promising rather than proven.

items.d: Increases dopamine production and protects dopamine neurons. Studied for motivation, drive and age-related cognitive decline.
items.x: Raises dopamine by increasing the enzyme that produces it, and appears to protect dopamine neurons rather than just stimulating them. Rodent work shows an increase in dopamine neuron count in the substantia nigra, the region affected in Parkinson's. Used for motivation and drive, with a neuroprotective rationale behind it.

items.d: Mild SARM with low suppression and some neuroprotective data.
items.x: A mild SARM with partial agonist activity, meaning it only partially activates the androgen receptor. Low suppression relative to the class, and some neuroprotective and cognitive data in animals. Weaker anabolic effect is the trade-off.

items.d: Synthetic peptide researched for hormone regulation and muscle wasting. Limited published data.
items.x: A synthetic peptide researched around hormone signalling and muscle-wasting models. Published literature is very limited — a handful of papers, no human data. Treat anything claimed about it with caution.

items.d: 0.6% acetic acid solution for reconstituting peptides that resist standard water.
items.x: A 0.6% acetic acid solution for reconstituting peptides that resist standard water. If a vial stays cloudy or has visible particles after adding bacteriostatic water, this is usually the reason. Check the specific peptide's requirement first.

items.d: Activates AMPK, the cellular energy sensor exercise switches on. Endurance and glucose disposal.
items.x: AMPK is the sensor that tells a cell it's running low on energy, and switching it on triggers the same adaptations as endurance training. It became famous as the original "exercise in a bottle" and is banned in competitive sport for that reason. Injectable only and expensive at effective doses, which is why it stays niche.

items.d: Highly absorbable choline that crosses into the brain. Raw material for acetylcholine, your focus and memory neurotransmitter.
items.x: A highly bioavailable choline source that crosses the blood-brain barrier, where it becomes acetylcholine — the neurotransmitter underpinning focus, memory and muscle activation. It also produces a short-term growth hormone bump, which is why it shows up in pre-workouts. Some observational data has raised stroke-risk questions at high chronic doses.

items.d: Tadalafil analog. PDE5 inhibitor for erectile blood flow, with a long duration.
items.x: A tadalafil analog working through the same PDE5 mechanism — it relaxes blood vessels to improve erectile blood flow, and lasts far longer than sildenafil. Because it's an analog rather than the pharmaceutical, consistency between batches varies. The nitrate interaction is the serious one; never combine with nitrates.

items.d: Fat-soluble racetam with a calming character. Used for creative thinking and reduced social anxiety.
items.x: A fat-soluble racetam that modulates AMPA receptors with a distinctly calming, anxiolytic character compared with other racetams. Often chosen for creative or verbal work rather than raw focus. Short half-life means multiple daily doses.

items.d: Modified fragment of growth hormone that targets fat burning only, without affecting blood sugar or IGF-1.
items.x: This is a modified version of the tail end of growth hormone, the part responsible for fat breakdown. Because the growth-signalling portion is removed, it doesn't raise IGF-1 or affect blood sugar the way full GH does. Human trials were underwhelming at the doses tested, so expect a mild effect rather than a dramatic one.

items.d: Non-blood-building EPO derivative. Targets nerve repair and neuropathic pain, especially small-fibre nerve damage.
items.x: A fragment of EPO that keeps the tissue-repair signalling but has none of the red-blood-cell effects, so it doesn't thicken the blood. It targets the innate repair receptor, which sits on nerve and immune cells. Most of the human work is in small-fibre neuropathy and sarcoidosis, where it showed real pain improvement.

items.d: Aromatase inhibitor. Lowers estrogen and can raise LH by reducing negative feedback.
items.x: A suicidal aromatase inhibitor — it binds the enzyme permanently rather than competitively. Lowering estrogen reduces negative feedback on the pituitary, which can raise LH and testosterone. Driving estrogen too low causes joint pain, poor lipids and low libido, so this is easy to overdo.

items.d: Direct cellular energy substrates plus N-acetyl-L-tyrosine, the raw material your body uses to make dopamine and adrenaline.
items.x: Combines direct cellular energy substrates with N-acetyl-L-tyrosine, the precursor your body uses to build dopamine and adrenaline. The tyrosine component is most useful under stress or sleep deprivation, when catecholamine production is the bottleneck. Typically used pre-training or for cognitive demand.

items.d: Pan-AMPK activator. Improves insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake, mimicking part of what exercise does.
items.x: A pan-AMPK activator, meaning it switches on all the AMPK subunits rather than just one. Research centres on insulin sensitivity, glucose uptake and vascular function in metabolic disease models. Very little human data exists, so this is early-stage.

items.d: Mitochondrial uncoupler. Raises calorie burn by releasing energy as heat rather than storing it.
items.x: Mitochondrial uncouplers let energy escape as heat instead of being captured as ATP, so you burn more calories at rest. This is the same mechanism as DNP, but BAM15 has a far wider safety margin because it doesn't affect the cell membrane the same way. Still, it's an uncoupler — the dose-response is steep and overheating is the known risk class.

items.d: The three branched-chain amino acids in liquid form, used around training for recovery and muscle-protein signalling.
items.x: The three branched-chain amino acids — leucine, isoleucine and valine — with leucine doing most of the muscle-protein signalling. Useful if total protein intake is low or you train fasted. If you're already eating adequate protein, the added benefit is small.

items.d: Amplifies your own dopamine and serotonin release rather than flooding the system. A successor to selegiline.
items.x: An activity enhancer rather than a releasing agent — it amplifies the neurotransmitter release that's already happening rather than forcing a dump. That mechanism means fewer crashes than classic stimulants. It's a successor to selegiline from the same research lineage, and far less studied.

items.d: The default injury stack: BPC-157 for local tissue repair, TB-500 for whole-body cell migration.
items.x: The two work on different parts of the same problem — BPC-157 drives local blood vessel and fibroblast activity, TB-500 moves cells into the area from further afield. That complementarity is why they're almost always run together for injuries. Typically dosed for 4-8 weeks around an acute injury rather than continuously.

items.d: Arginine salt of BPC-157, noticeably more stable than the standard form, with added nitric oxide support.
items.x: The arginine salt form, which is far more stable in solution than the acetate version and survives longer once reconstituted. The arginine counterion also contributes some nitric oxide, which may help blood flow to the area. Often sold as PDA or pentadeca arginate.

items.d: Raises dopamine by increasing the enzyme that makes it, so you get stimulation and drive without the crash or depletion.
items.x: Raises dopamine by upregulating the gene for tyrosine hydroxylase, the enzyme that makes it. Because you're producing more rather than releasing stored dopamine, there's no depletion or crash. Developed as an actoprotector for Soviet athletes, it has an unusual combination of stimulant and anxiolytic effects.

items.d: Lung and bronchial bioregulator peptide.
items.x: A short bioregulator peptide targeting lung and bronchial tissue. The cell-culture work is some of the better-quantified in the bioregulator family, with markers improving more in older cultures than younger ones. No human data exists.

items.d: Long-acting amylin analog. Slows stomach emptying and increases fullness, usually run alongside a GLP-1.
items.x: A long-acting amylin analog. Amylin slows stomach emptying and signals satiety through a different pathway than GLP-1, which is why the two stack well. On its own the weight loss is moderate; paired with semaglutide it approaches tirzepatide territory.

items.d: Cagrilintide and semaglutide together, hitting the amylin and GLP-1 pathways at the same time.
items.x: Cagrilintide and semaglutide in one vial, hitting amylin and GLP-1 at once. Trial results put it among the strongest weight-loss combinations tested. Because you are stacking two appetite pathways, titration matters more than usual — nausea is the common early complaint.

items.d: Heart muscle bioregulator peptide.
items.x: A bioregulator peptide for heart muscle tissue. The published research is almost entirely inside patent filings rather than peer-reviewed journals, and the one properly published result was in skin-type cells rather than cardiac. Thin evidence even by bioregulator standards.

items.d: Carnitine to shuttle fat into the mitochondria, arginine as a nitric-oxide precursor for blood flow.
items.x: Carnitine shuttles fat into the mitochondria to be burned; arginine is a nitric oxide precursor for blood flow. The pairing targets fat utilisation and delivery at once. Carnitine works best when insulin is present, so timing with a meal matters.

items.d: Carnitine for fat transport plus choline, the building block of acetylcholine and cell membranes.
items.x: Carnitine for fat transport plus choline for acetylcholine and cell membrane synthesis. The combination covers both the metabolic and the neuromuscular side. Commonly used in fat loss protocols as support rather than a driver.

items.d: Carnosine buffers the acid build-up that limits hard sets; carnitine moves fat into the mitochondria to be burned.
items.x: Carnosine buffers the hydrogen ions that build up during hard training and cause the burn that ends a set; carnitine moves fat into the mitochondria. One targets performance, the other substrate use. Carnosine's effect is cumulative over weeks, not acute.

items.d: Cartilage bioregulator peptide. Targets chondrocyte function and joint tissue.
items.x: A short bioregulator peptide targeting cartilage tissue. Research is confined to cell culture — chondrocyte behaviour and the inflammatory profile of aging cartilage. There is no animal or human data, and the osteoarthritis trials you may read about were run on a cartilage extract, not this peptide.

items.d: Cartalax layered onto BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV. A joint-focused version of the KLOW repair stack.
items.x: Cartalax layered onto the standard BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV repair stack, aimed at joints specifically. The logic is tissue-repair signalling plus a cartilage-directed bioregulator. It's a vendor formulation rather than a studied combination.

items.d: Choline source that also supplies uridine for building brain cell membranes. Gentler and longer-acting than alpha-GPC.
items.x: A choline source that also supplies cytidine, which the body converts to uridine for building brain cell membranes. That dual action makes it more structural and longer-acting than alpha-GPC. It has reasonable human trial data in stroke recovery and age-related cognitive decline.

items.d: Bioregulator sold for lungs, though the published research is on stomach lining repair.
items.x: Sold as a lung bioregulator, but every retrievable experiment on it is about the stomach — an ulcer model with H. pylori, where it performed comparably to an antibiotic. There appear to be two similarly-named organ extracts and the marketing picked the wrong one. If you want it for gut lining, the data supports that; for lungs, it doesn't.

items.d: GHRH analog without DAC. Short-acting, produces a clean natural GH pulse. Usually paired with a GHRP.
items.x: A GHRH analog without the DAC attachment, so it clears quickly and produces a short, natural-shaped GH pulse rather than a constant elevation. That pulsatile pattern is closer to normal physiology. Almost always paired with a GHRP, since the two together produce a much larger release than either alone.

items.d: GHRH analog without DAC. Short-acting, produces a clean natural GH pulse. Usually paired with a GHRP.
items.x: A GHRH analog without the DAC attachment, so it clears quickly and produces a short, natural-shaped GH pulse rather than a constant elevation. That pulsatile pattern is closer to normal physiology. Almost always paired with a GHRP, since the two together produce a much larger release than either alone.

items.d: The standard growth hormone pairing. One drives the pulse, the other amplifies it, with minimal cortisol or prolactin.
items.x: The default growth hormone pairing. One tells the pituitary to release, the other amplifies how much comes out, and together they produce a pulse neither achieves alone. Ipamorelin's selectivity means minimal cortisol, prolactin or hunger spike. Usually run before bed to ride the natural overnight pulse.

items.d: Derived from fisetin. Protects brain cells by reducing fat oxidation damage in the aging brain.
items.x: Derived from fisetin, a flavonoid. It inhibits fatty acid synthase, which reduces the lipid peroxidation that damages brain cells during aging. Part of a series of compounds developed specifically as geroneuroprotectors. Preclinical only.

items.d: A proprietary repair blend. Exact composition isn't published.
items.x: A proprietary repair blend. The exact composition isn't published, which makes it hard to say much with confidence. If you're choosing between this and a named blend, the named one is easier to reason about.

items.d: Mitochondrial electron carrier and fat-soluble antioxidant. Heart and cellular energy support.
items.x: A component of the electron transport chain, the final step of cellular energy production, and a fat-soluble antioxidant. Levels drop with age and are notably depleted by statins. Most useful where mitochondrial energy is the bottleneck — heart function and statin-related muscle complaints.

items.d: Pushes cells to burn glucose in the mitochondria instead of fermenting it. A metabolic reset mechanism.
items.x: Blocks the enzyme that keeps pyruvate out of the mitochondria, pushing cells to fully oxidise glucose rather than ferment it to lactate. Researched for metabolic and mitochondrial conditions. Human data is limited and mostly from outside the West.

items.d: Extremely potent synaptogenic compound derived from angiotensin IV. Builds new connections between neurons.
items.x: Derived from angiotensin IV, and reported to be orders of magnitude more potent than BDNF at driving new synapse formation. It crosses the blood-brain barrier readily. That potency is the concern as much as the appeal — indiscriminate synaptogenesis is not obviously desirable, and there's no human data.

items.d: Potent stimulant. Sharp energy and appetite suppression, with a strong effect on blood pressure.
items.x: A potent stimulant that works through noradrenaline release, producing sharp focus and appetite suppression. It was pulled from the US supplement market over cardiovascular safety concerns. Blood pressure response is significant and stacking it with other stimulants is where people get into trouble.

items.d: Delta sleep-inducing peptide. Promotes deep slow-wave sleep and dampens the stress axis.
items.x: Delta sleep-inducing peptide promotes slow-wave sleep — the deep, physically restorative stage rather than total sleep time. It also modulates the stress axis. Results are notably inconsistent between individuals, with some people reporting a clear effect and others nothing at all.

items.d: Russian antioxidant and membrane stabiliser used for anxiety, stress tolerance and low-oxygen protection.
items.x: A Russian antioxidant and membrane stabiliser used widely there for anxiety, stress tolerance and protection against low oxygen. It stabilises neuronal membranes rather than acting on a specific receptor. Most literature is Russian-language and hasn't been independently replicated.

items.d: Pure isomer of clomiphene. Raises LH, FSH and natural testosterone while preserving fertility.
items.x: The pure trans-isomer of clomiphene, separated out because the other isomer causes most of the mood and visual side effects. It blocks estrogen receptors at the pituitary, which raises LH, FSH and natural testosterone while preserving fertility. That fertility preservation is what makes it the preferred option over TRT for men who want children.

items.d: Alternate spelling of Epitalon. Pineal peptide for telomere support and sleep rhythm.
items.x: Alternate spelling of Epitalon, the same four-amino-acid pineal peptide. Used for telomere support and restoring melatonin rhythm. Note the frequently-cited human mortality data belongs to Epithalamin, a pineal extract, not to this synthetic peptide.

items.d: Modafinil-family wakefulness compound. Alertness and focus without classic stimulant jitter.
items.x: A modafinil analog producing wakefulness and focus without classic stimulant jitter. Reported to be less aggression-promoting than adrafinil, though that comparison rests on anecdote more than data. Like all eugeroics, it works best as an occasional tool rather than a daily one.

items.d: Anxiolytic peptide acting on cholecystokinin receptors. Calming without benzodiazepine-style sedation.
items.x: A synthetic retro-analog of a cholecystokinin fragment, producing anxiety relief without benzodiazepine-style sedation or dependence. Developed in Russia. The published work is limited and largely untranslated.

items.d: Liver-selective thyroid hormone agonist. Lowers lipids and raises fat burning without the heart strain of T3.
items.x: Thyroid hormone drives fat loss but also strains the heart. GC-1 was designed to activate the thyroid receptor mainly in the liver, lowering cholesterol and raising fat oxidation without the same cardiac load. Human trials exist for lipid lowering; it is still not an approved drug anywhere.

items.d: The flagship skin peptide. Copper-binding tripeptide driving collagen production, wound healing and hair follicle signalling.
items.x: A copper-binding tripeptide found naturally in plasma, with levels declining sharply with age. It drives collagen and elastin production, wound remodelling and hair follicle signalling. It's among the best-evidenced cosmetic peptides, with real topical data. Injected forms carry more systemic copper, which is worth considering.

items.d: Copper peptide repair paired with KPV's anti-inflammatory action.
items.x: Copper peptide for collagen and tissue remodelling paired with KPV's anti-inflammatory action. Used where repair and inflammation both need addressing — skin conditions and gut protocols most often. A smaller, more targeted blend than GLOW or KLOW.

items.d: GHK-Cu and methylene blue in a tallow base for topical application.
items.x: Copper peptide and methylene blue suspended in a tallow base for topical use. Combines collagen and skin-repair signalling with methylene blue's mitochondrial and antimicrobial activity. A formulation choice rather than a studied combination.

items.d: The flagship skin peptide. Copper-binding tripeptide driving collagen production, wound healing and hair follicle signalling.
items.x: A copper-binding tripeptide found naturally in plasma, with levels declining sharply with age. It drives collagen and elastin production, wound remodelling and hair follicle signalling. It's among the best-evidenced cosmetic peptides, with real topical data. Injected forms carry more systemic copper, which is worth considering.

items.d: GHK-Cu, TB-500 and BPC-157 together. The go-to stack for skin, hair and connective tissue.
items.x: GHK-Cu, TB-500 and BPC-157 together — copper peptide for collagen and skin, plus the two repair peptides. It's the most popular cosmetic-plus-recovery stack, used for skin quality, hair and connective tissue. The copper peptide is what makes it a skin protocol rather than purely an injury one.

items.d: The body's master antioxidant, injected. Used for detox pathways, liver support and skin brightening.
items.x: The body's primary antioxidant, central to liver detoxification pathways. Oral glutathione is largely destroyed in digestion, which is why injectable and acetylated forms exist. Commonly used for liver support and skin brightening, the latter being a well-documented side effect of the same mechanism.

items.d: More selective PPAR-delta agonist than Cardarine, with a similar endurance and lipid profile.
items.x: A more selective PPAR-delta agonist than Cardarine, with a similar endurance and lipid profile. Less widely used and correspondingly less characterised. Same mechanism, same open questions.

items.d: PPAR-delta agonist. Dramatic endurance gains and fat oxidation; carries rodent cancer data at very high doses.
items.x: A PPAR-delta agonist that dramatically increases endurance and fat oxidation by shifting muscle toward burning fat. Development was halted when rodents developed cancers across multiple organs at high chronic doses. Those doses were far above typical use, but it's the reason it was abandoned and why WADA bans it.

items.d: The most powerful GHRP by peak GH release, but it desensitises fastest. Short cycles only.
items.x: The strongest GHRP by peak GH release, but it desensitises the receptor faster than any other. Run it continuously and the effect fades within weeks. Short, intermittent blocks are the standard approach, and it carries more prolactin and cortisol than ipamorelin.

items.d: Maximum-amplitude growth hormone pulse. Powerful but desensitises quickly.
items.x: Pairs the most potent GHRP with a GHRH analog for the largest possible pulse. Powerful, but hexarelin's rapid desensitisation means this isn't something to run continuously. Short cycles with real breaks.

items.d: The fat-burning tail end of growth hormone, isolated. Lipolysis without growth signalling.
items.x: The last 15 amino acids of growth hormone, isolated because that fragment carries the fat-burning activity without the growth signalling. In theory you get lipolysis with no effect on IGF-1, blood sugar or tissue growth. In practice human results have been modest, and it's typically run alongside a GH secretagogue rather than alone.

items.d: Modified IGF-1 that stays active far longer in the body. Muscle growth and recovery.
items.x: IGF-1 is what growth hormone actually signals through to build tissue. The LR3 modification stops binding proteins from clearing it, so it stays active dramatically longer than natural IGF-1. That potency cuts both ways — it drives growth indiscriminately, which is why blood sugar and tissue-growth concerns come up.

items.d: Lipophilic antioxidant that concentrates in the mitochondria to scavenge free radicals in brain tissue.
items.x: A lipophilic indole derivative that concentrates in mitochondria, where it scavenges free radicals non-enzymatically. Different mechanism from most antioxidants, which need enzymes to work. Research is focused on neuroprotection.

items.d: The cleanest growth hormone secretagogue. Raises GH with essentially no cortisol, prolactin or hunger spike.
items.x: The cleanest of the GH secretagogues. It triggers GH release through the ghrelin receptor but, unlike older GHRPs, barely touches cortisol, prolactin or appetite. That selectivity is the entire reason it's the default choice. Effects are real but gradual — think sleep and recovery over weeks, not a dramatic change.

items.d: Shifts haemoglobin to release more oxygen into tissue. Endurance research.
items.x: Shifts haemoglobin's oxygen binding so it releases more oxygen into tissue rather than holding onto it. Studied for endurance, ischemia and tumour oxygenation. It's on the WADA banned list, which tells you the performance effect is considered real.

items.d: Curcumin derivative with far better absorption. Raises BDNF and targets the mitochondria; a leading anti-aging brain compound.
items.x: A curcumin derivative engineered for the bioavailability curcumin itself lacks. It raises BDNF and targets mitochondrial ATP synthase, and is one of the better-performing compounds in Alzheimer's mouse models. It has entered early human trials, which is more than most compounds here.

items.d: Ten-amino-acid kisspeptin. Stimulates the natural LH/FSH cascade and libido.
items.x: The ten-amino-acid fragment, the form most commonly used. Stimulates the natural LH and FSH cascade and is studied in fertility and hypogonadism contexts. Short half-life means timing matters.

items.d: GLOW with KPV added for the anti-inflammatory and gut arm. A four-peptide repair matrix.
items.x: GLOW with KPV added, which brings an anti-inflammatory and gut-directed component to the repair trio. Four peptides covering tissue repair, skin and inflammation. Popular as a general recovery protocol rather than for a specific injury.

items.d: The active tail of alpha-MSH. A potent anti-inflammatory, and the first choice for gut inflammation.
items.x: The last three amino acids of alpha-MSH, which turn out to carry most of its anti-inflammatory activity without the pigmentation effects. It acts on NF-kB, a master inflammatory switch. The strongest case for it is gut inflammation, where it works locally on the lining.

items.d: Selective adenosine A2A blocker. Caffeine's target, hit cleanly, for motivation and motor drive.
items.x: A second-generation adenosine A2A receptor antagonist — the same target caffeine hits, but selectively and without caffeine's other actions. A2A blockade raises dopamine signalling, which translates to motivation and motor drive. Developed for Parkinson's rather than as a nootropic.

items.d: Arginine-based nitric oxide precursor. Vasodilation, blood flow and pump.
items.x: Arginine is the direct precursor to nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels and improves blood flow. Oral arginine is heavily degraded before it reaches circulation, which is why citrulline often works better; the injectable route avoids that problem.

items.d: Carries long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondria so they can actually be burned for fuel.
items.x: Carnitine's job is carrying long-chain fatty acids across the mitochondrial membrane so they can be burned. Without enough of it, fat can't reach the furnace. Oral absorption is poor and saturable, which is the main argument for the injectable form.

items.d: Citrulline raises arginine levels more reliably than arginine itself, for longer-lasting nitric oxide and blood flow.
items.x: Citrulline raises blood arginine levels more effectively than arginine itself, because it skips the liver breakdown that destroys most oral arginine. The result is longer-lasting nitric oxide and better blood flow. The counterintuitive one — citrulline beats arginine for raising arginine.

items.d: Alkaloid from corydalis. Analgesic and sedative, studied for pain and stimulant craving.
items.x: An alkaloid from corydalis, used in Chinese medicine for centuries. It blocks dopamine D1 and D2 receptors, producing analgesia and sedation. Studied for stimulant craving and chronic pain. Being a dopamine antagonist, it is not a nootropic in the stimulating sense — expect the opposite.

items.d: Second-generation ligandrol with a more tissue-selective profile and notable bone density data.
items.x: A second-generation ligandrol analog with a more tissue-selective profile and notable bone density data in animals. The intent was keeping the anabolic effect while reducing suppression. Human data is minimal.

items.d: High-affinity SARM with the best-documented lean mass gains of the class. Reliably suppressive.
items.x: A high-affinity SARM with the best-documented lean mass gains in the class, including human trial data showing meaningful increases over a few weeks. It reliably suppresses natural testosterone, and suppression scales with dose and duration. Recovery timelines vary.

items.d: Lipotropic fat-metabolism blend with added B12 for energy.
items.x: A lipotropic blend with added B12 for the energy side. Used weekly alongside a deficit, usually in combination with a GLP-1 rather than instead of one. Benefits are supportive rather than dramatic.

items.d: Liver bioregulator peptide. Also loosens packed-up DNA in aged immune cells.
items.x: A liver-directed bioregulator peptide. Cell work shows it has the strongest DNA binding of the bioregulator family and loosens packed chromatin in aged immune cells. The hepatitis patient data circulating for it exists only in a patent filing, not a peer-reviewed journal.

items.d: Human antimicrobial defence peptide. Broad antibacterial activity plus biofilm disruption and immune modulation.
items.x: A human antimicrobial peptide, part of your innate immune defence. It kills bacteria directly, breaks up biofilms that shield them from antibiotics, and modulates the immune response. The biofilm activity is the distinctive part — it's used in chronic infection protocols where standard antibiotics stall.

items.d: Semaglutide. Single GLP-1 receptor agonist, taken weekly.
items.x: Semaglutide mimics GLP-1, slowing gastric emptying, reducing appetite and improving insulin sensitivity. Weekly injection with a gradual dose increase to manage nausea. The most thoroughly studied compound in the category.

items.d: Tirzepatide. Dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist, generally stronger than semaglutide for weight loss.
items.x: Tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, and in direct comparison produces more weight loss than semaglutide. Weekly dosing, titrated upward over months. Nausea, reflux and constipation are the usual early complaints and generally settle.

items.d: Retatrutide. Triple agonist on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon, with the largest weight loss of the class in trials.
items.x: Retatrutide is a triple agonist — GLP-1 and GIP for appetite, plus glucagon to raise energy expenditure. Trial participants lost more weight than on any previous incretin. It remains investigational, and the glucagon arm means heart rate and liver markers are worth watching.

items.d: Retatrutide with cagrilintide in one vial, adding amylin to the triple agonist.
items.x: Retatrutide paired with cagrilintide in a single vial, layering amylin on top of the triple agonist. Aimed at maximum appetite suppression with better lean-mass preservation. No clinical trial has evaluated this specific combination.

items.d: The only magnesium form that meaningfully raises magnesium inside the brain. Used for synapse density and sleep quality.
items.x: The only magnesium form shown to meaningfully raise magnesium concentration inside the brain, which ordinary magnesium supplements don't achieve. Research centres on synapse density and sleep quality. If you're taking magnesium for sleep or cognition specifically, the form matters.

items.d: Antibody-peptide conjugate built for monthly rather than weekly dosing. Blocks GIP while activating GLP-1.
items.x: Built as an antibody-peptide conjugate, which gives it a much longer half-life than a standard peptide — monthly rather than weekly. Unusually, it blocks GIP while activating GLP-1, the opposite of tirzepatide's approach, and both strategies appear to work. Still in trials.

items.d: Dual GLP-1 and glucagon agonist. The glucagon arm adds calorie burn on top of appetite suppression.
items.x: Activates GLP-1 and glucagon receptors. The glucagon component raises energy expenditure and has shown liver-fat benefits alongside weight loss. Developed primarily in China, where most of the trial data comes from.

items.d: Non-selective melanocortin agonist. Tanning plus a strong libido effect; nausea and mole darkening are the trade-offs.
items.x: A non-selective melanocortin agonist, so it hits MC1R for tanning and MC4R for libido simultaneously. Nausea and facial flushing are common early, and it can darken existing moles — worth a skin check before and after. The non-selectivity is both why it does more than MT-1 and why it's less comfortable.

items.d: Liquid melatonin blend for sleep onset and circadian timing.
items.x: Liquid melatonin for sleep onset and circadian timing. Melatonin is a timing signal rather than a sedative, so it works best taken a few hours before target sleep time, and low doses often outperform high ones. More is not better here.

items.d: Nootropic blend in a dissolving oral strip.
items.x: A nootropic blend in a sublingual strip. Formulation varies — check the product page for what's in it. Convenient format, with the usual caveat that sublingual absorption is less consistent than injection or intranasal.

items.d: NAD+ in a dissolving oral strip, avoiding the flush that comes with injecting it.
items.x: NAD+ in a strip that dissolves under the tongue, which avoids both the injection and the intense flush that IV NAD+ causes. Absorption is lower than injection, so this is a maintenance format rather than a loading one. Convenient enough for daily use.

items.d: Semax and Selank together in a dissolving oral strip. Focus and drive paired with an anxiolytic.
items.x: Semax and Selank in a sublingual strip — one for drive and focus, the other to take the edge off. The pairing is popular precisely because the stimulation and the calm offset each other. Sublingual absorption is less reliable than intranasal or injection.

items.n: Melts Pro CJC 1295 Ipamorelin Dissolving Strips
items.d: The standard GH pairing in a dissolving oral strip, no injection required.
items.x: The standard GH secretagogue pairing in a strip that dissolves under the tongue. Convenient if needles are the barrier. Sublingual absorption of peptides this size is less reliable than injection, so expect a weaker effect than the injectable version.

items.n: Melts Pro Melanotan Ii Dissolving Strips
items.d: Melanotan 2 in a dissolving oral strip, no injection needed.
items.x: Melanotan 2 in a sublingual strip, avoiding injections. Expect the same nausea and flushing, since those are systemic rather than route-dependent. Absorption is less predictable than injection, which makes dialling in a dose harder.

items.n: Melts Pro Tesofensine 5 Amino 1mq Dissolving Strips
items.d: Tesofensine and 5-Amino-1MQ in a dissolving strip, pairing appetite suppression with fat-cell metabolism.
items.x: Pairs a strong central appetite suppressant with an NNMT inhibitor that works on the fat cell itself, in a strip that dissolves under the tongue. The format avoids injections and first-pass metabolism. Tesofensine is the active half here and carries a real stimulant load — blood pressure and sleep are the things to watch.

items.d: Sleep blend in a dissolving oral strip.
items.x: A sleep blend in a strip that dissolves under the tongue, bypassing digestion for faster onset. Formulations vary — check what's in it. Sublingual is a sensible route for sleep compounds specifically, since speed matters.

items.d: At low doses, a mitochondrial electron carrier that improves cellular energy production. Also antimicrobial.
items.x: At low doses it acts as an alternative electron carrier in the mitochondria, bypassing bottlenecks in energy production. At higher doses it becomes an MAO inhibitor, which creates real interaction risk with SSRIs and other serotonergic drugs. Dose matters enormously here — low is the therapeutic window.

items.d: The mildest and most studied SARM. Recomposition and joint support with the least suppression.
items.x: The mildest and most studied SARM, with multiple human trials in muscle wasting. It produces modest lean mass gains with the least suppression of the group, and users frequently report joint relief. The low-risk entry point of the category, though still suppressive.

items.d: Oral growth hormone secretagogue. Raises GH and IGF-1 around the clock; expect hunger and water retention.
items.x: An orally active ghrelin mimetic that raises GH and IGF-1 around the clock rather than in pulses. That constant elevation is both its appeal and its drawback — it works, but it also drives serious hunger, water retention and some insulin resistance. Most people find the appetite effect the deciding factor.

items.d: Newer orally active growth hormone secretagogue in the MK series. Limited public data.
items.x: A newer orally active GH secretagogue in the same family as MK-677. Positioned as having a cleaner profile, though there's very little published data to confirm that. Early and largely unvalidated.

items.d: Mitochondrial peptide that activates AMPK. Improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic flexibility; an exercise mimetic.
items.x: A peptide encoded by mitochondrial DNA rather than the nucleus, which is unusual. It activates AMPK and appears to improve how flexibly the body switches between burning carbs and fat. Levels decline with age, and most research is in metabolic and exercise-capacity models rather than weight loss specifically.

items.d: Methylsulfonylmethane, a sulfur donor used for joint comfort and connective tissue.
items.x: Methylsulfonylmethane is a sulfur donor, and sulfur is structural in connective tissue and cartilage. Used for joint comfort and skin. Reasonable human data for osteoarthritis symptoms at adequate doses.

items.d: Central cellular energy cofactor and sirtuin fuel. Declines steeply with age.
items.x: The central cofactor for energy production and the fuel sirtuins need to do DNA repair. Levels fall substantially with age, and restoring them is one of the better-supported ideas in longevity. Injected or IV NAD+ causes a distinctive flushing sensation that's dose-rate dependent — go slow.

items.d: NAD+ paired with carnitine, combining cellular energy with fat transport.
items.x: Pairs NAD+ with carnitine, combining the cellular energy cofactor with the molecule that transports fat into the mitochondria to be burned. The logic is addressing both the fuel delivery and the machinery. Commonly run as part of a metabolic or energy protocol.

items.d: Racetam acting on NMDA and cholinergic channels. Studied for post-stroke apathy and mood.
items.x: A racetam acting on NMDA receptors and calcium channels rather than purely AMPA. Studied specifically for post-stroke apathy and mood rather than raw cognition. Animal toxicity findings at high doses halted some development.

items.d: Glutamic acid derivative with anti-amnestic and neuroprotective effects.
items.x: A glutamic acid derivative with anti-amnestic and neuroprotective effects, acting on AMPA receptors. From the Russian nootropic research programme. Limited Western replication.

items.d: Dipeptide nootropic roughly a thousand times stronger than piracetam by weight. Raises BDNF and NGF.
items.x: A dipeptide roughly a thousand times more potent than piracetam by weight, so doses are in the tens of milligrams. It converts to cycloprolylglycine, which raises BDNF and NGF. Among the better-evidenced nootropics with human trial data, and fast-acting enough to feel.

items.d: Tadalafil analog working through the same PDE5 mechanism.
items.x: A demethylated tadalafil analog using the same PDE5 mechanism for erectile blood flow. As an analog rather than the pharmaceutical, potency varies between batches. The nitrate contraindication applies in full.

items.d: Grows new neurons in the hippocampus and increases its volume. An antidepressant mechanism that doesn't work through serotonin.
items.x: Stimulates the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus and has been shown to increase hippocampal volume. That's an antidepressant mechanism entirely separate from serotonin. It reached phase II trials, where it missed its primary endpoint but improved secondary cognitive measures.

items.d: Bioregulator sold for ovarian and liver support, though the published research describes kidney function.
items.x: Sold as an ovarian or liver bioregulator, but the published research describes kidney cell function. Adding to the confusion, Ovagen is also the name of an unrelated veterinary fertility drug, which makes searching for it difficult. If you want it for ovarian support, the evidence isn't there.

items.d: The bonding hormone. Social connection, trust and orgasmic response.
items.x: The bonding hormone, involved in social connection, trust and orgasmic response. Typically used intranasally for the social and mood effects, since that route reaches the brain more directly. Effects are context-dependent — it tends to amplify existing social feeling rather than create it.

items.d: Synthetic version of a nerve growth factor. Promotes new brain cell growth without the side effects of the natural protein.
items.x: A synthetic analog of ciliary neurotrophic factor, designed to deliver the neurogenic benefits without the side effects of the natural protein. It promotes new brain cell growth in the hippocampus. Preclinical only, with no human data.

items.d: Blocks the TREK-1 channel, a fast-acting antidepressant mechanism that also encourages new neuron growth.
items.x: An analog of spadin that blocks the TREK-1 potassium channel — a fast-acting antidepressant mechanism that also encourages new neuron growth. The appeal is speed; TREK-1 blockade works in days rather than the weeks SSRIs need. Animal data only.

items.d: Naturally occurring fatty acid amide. Non-opioid pain relief and anti-inflammatory action, particularly for nerve pain.
items.x: A fatty acid amide your body already makes, which rises naturally in response to tissue damage. It works through PPAR-alpha to calm the immune cells that amplify pain signals, particularly nerve pain. Human trials are reasonably solid for chronic and neuropathic pain, and it's non-opioid with a clean safety record.

items.d: The full name for BPC-157, a fifteen-amino-acid peptide for tissue and gut repair.
items.x: Another name for BPC-157, so called because it's fifteen amino acids long. Same compound, same mechanism — angiogenesis and fibroblast migration for tendon, ligament and gut repair. Worth knowing the alias so you don't buy the same thing twice.

items.d: Long-acting amylin analog designed to be more lean-mass-sparing than GLP-1s alone.
items.x: A long-acting amylin analog designed to be stable enough for weekly dosing. The appeal is that amylin-driven weight loss appears to spare more lean mass than GLP-1-driven loss. Early-stage compared with the established incretins.

items.d: Strong anxiety relief and sociability via GABA-B. Tolerance builds fast and withdrawal is real, so strictly occasional use.
items.x: A GABA-B agonist producing strong anxiety relief and sociability. It genuinely works, which is the problem — tolerance builds within days and withdrawal from regular use is severe and medically significant. If you use it, strictly occasional with multi-day gaps, never daily.

items.d: Phenylpiracetam variant that skews calming rather than stimulating, while keeping the memory benefits.
items.x: A modified phenylpiracetam where the hydrazide group shifts the profile toward calm rather than stimulation while retaining the memory effects. Useful if standard phenylpiracetam is too activating. Longer-acting than the parent compound.

items.d: pH-balanced saline diluent, used where bacteriostatic water would degrade the peptide.
items.x: pH-balanced saline for reconstituting peptides sensitive to pH shifts. Also more comfortable to inject than acidic diluents. Not a universal replacement for bacteriostatic water — it has no preservative.

items.d: Brain bioregulator peptide. Neuroprotection and cognitive aging research.
items.x: A three-amino-acid brain bioregulator. The best-designed study — an Alzheimer's mouse model — had its primary endpoint come back negative, though neuron connection density improved modestly. Notably, a rat study found the middle dose outperformed the highest, which is a direct argument against assuming more is better.

items.d: The original nootropic. Mild, broad support for memory and mental clarity.
items.x: The original nootropic and the compound that coined the term. It modulates AMPA receptors and improves cell membrane fluidity. Effects are mild and cumulative rather than acute — most people notice little day to day. Doses are large, measured in grams.

items.d: Best documented for a dramatic improvement in verbal memory and word recall.
items.x: A phenylmethylamine derivative with unusually specific evidence: a human trial showed dramatic improvement in verbal retention and word recall, particularly in people with below-average baseline memory. Very long-acting relative to its short half-life, suggesting a downstream mechanism. Limited research beyond that original work.

items.d: Prostate bioregulator peptide.
items.x: A prostate-directed bioregulator peptide. The substantial Russian clinical research on prostate peptides was done on Prostatilen, a bovine prostate extract, not on this synthetic peptide. What exists for the peptide itself is cell-culture work and patent filings.

items.d: Works centrally on desire pathways rather than blood flow, so it addresses libido itself. Effective for both sexes.
items.x: Unlike Viagra and its relatives, this works in the brain on melanocortin receptors rather than on blood flow, so it acts on desire itself rather than mechanics. That makes it effective for both men and women, and it's approved as Vyleesi for low desire in women. Nausea is the common side effect, and it raises blood pressure transiently.

items.d: GHK-Cu with NAD+. Repair signalling plus cellular energy in one vial.
items.x: GHK-Cu paired with NAD+ — copper peptide for collagen and tissue remodelling alongside the central energy cofactor. Repair signalling plus the cellular energy to act on it. A convenience blend rather than a studied combination.

items.d: Potent SARM with a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio. Strong suppression and some liver strain reported.
items.x: A potent SARM with a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio in animal models. Strong suppression is expected, and there are case reports of liver injury at higher doses and longer runs. More aggressive than LGD-4033 in both effect and side effect profile.

items.d: Ester-modified RAD-140 that stays active longer in the body.
items.x: An ester-modified RAD-140 designed to stay active longer in the body. Same underlying compound, slower release. Even less human data than RAD-140, which is already limited.

items.d: Diluent for turning lyophilised powder into an injectable solution.
items.x: The diluent used to turn lyophilised powder into an injectable solution. Add it slowly down the inside wall of the vial and swirl gently; never shake, as agitation damages peptide structure. Which diluent to use depends on the peptide.

items.d: Acetylated glutathione that survives digestion and reaches the cell intact. Oral master antioxidant.
items.x: Standard oral glutathione is broken down before absorption. The acetylated form survives digestion and reaches the cell intact, where the acetyl group is removed. That makes it a genuine oral option rather than a waste of money.

items.d: Partial-agonist SARM known for hardening and fat loss. The yellow vision tint is dose-dependent and reverses.
items.x: A partial agonist SARM known for a hardening, drying visual effect and some fat loss. Its distinctive side effect is a yellow tint to vision and difficulty adjusting to darkness, caused by binding in the retina — dose-dependent and fully reversible on stopping. That visual effect is why it fell out of favour.

items.d: Anxiolytic peptide that calms without sedation or cognitive fog, while supporting memory via BDNF.
items.x: A synthetic analog of tuftsin, an immune peptide. It reduces anxiety without sedation or cognitive dulling and raises BDNF, so it supports memory at the same time. Typically intranasal. One of the better-tolerated anxiolytics with no dependence profile.

items.d: Orexin receptor blocker. A newer sleep mechanism that works by switching off wakefulness rather than sedating you.
items.x: An orexin receptor antagonist — it blocks the signal that keeps you awake rather than sedating you into sleep. That's a fundamentally different and generally cleaner mechanism than benzodiazepines or Z-drugs, with less next-day grogginess and no dependence profile. It has been through phase III trials for insomnia with depression.

items.d: Raises BDNF and nerve growth factor. Used for focus, mental stamina and neuroprotection.
items.x: An analog of a fragment of ACTH, stripped of the hormonal activity. It raises BDNF and nerve growth factor, supporting focus, mental stamina and neuroprotection. Used in Russia for stroke recovery. Usually intranasal, and most people notice it within a session rather than over weeks.

items.d: The classic stack: Semax for drive and focus, Selank to take the edge off.
items.x: The classic nootropic pairing — Semax for drive and focus, Selank to blunt the overstimulation. They're frequently run together because the combination is better balanced than either alone. Both are typically intranasal.

items.d: The original GHRH fragment. Very short-acting and mild, producing a natural GH pulse pattern.
items.x: The original GHRH fragment, and the mildest option here. Its very short half-life means a brief, natural pulse with no accumulation. Often used as a starting point or in clinical anti-aging settings where a gentle approach is preferred.

items.d: Exercise mimetic that activates ERR-alpha, raising fat oxidation and mitochondrial production in muscle.
items.x: ERR-alpha is one of the master switches muscle flips on during endurance exercise. Activating it chemically raises fat oxidation and mitochondrial production without the training. Mouse studies showed meaningful fat loss without diet change; there is no human data yet, which is the key caveat.

items.d: Next-generation SLU-PP compound hitting all three ERR receptors for broader metabolic activation.
items.x: A newer compound in the same series that activates all three ERR receptors rather than just alpha, broadening the metabolic effect. Positioned as a more complete exercise mimetic than SLU-PP-332. Even earlier in development, with correspondingly less data.

items.d: REV-ERB agonist affecting circadian and mitochondrial genes. Oral absorption is poor, hence the oil format.
items.x: A REV-ERB agonist affecting circadian and mitochondrial gene expression, which is why it's marketed as exercise in a bottle. Oral bioavailability is extremely poor, so most oral products do very little — hence the oil format. The impressive rodent data used injection.

items.d: Extremely potent ampakine active at microgram doses. Memory and learning.
items.x: An ampakine active at microgram doses, which makes it one of the most potent compounds in the category by weight. It positively modulates AMPA and NMDA receptors. Potency plus almost no safety data is a meaningful caution — accurate dosing is non-trivial at this scale.

items.d: Selective AMPA receptor potentiator without the seizure risk of older ampakines. Fast antidepressant signal.
items.x: A selective AMPA receptor potentiator engineered to avoid the seizure liability that stalled earlier ampakines. It produces fast antidepressant signals in trials without the dissociative effects of ketamine. Among the more rigorously developed compounds in this category.

items.d: Actin-regulating peptide that drives cell migration and blood vessel growth throughout the body. The systemic partner to BPC-157.
items.x: A synthetic version of a region of thymosin beta-4, the protein that regulates actin and therefore cell movement. It promotes cell migration and blood vessel growth throughout the body, which makes it the systemic counterpart to BPC-157's local action. Animal data for wound and cardiac repair is good; human data is thin.

items.d: The only GH secretagogue with clinical data specifically on reducing visceral belly fat.
items.x: A stabilised GHRH analog, and the only GH secretagogue with clinical trial data specifically showing reduced visceral fat — the deep abdominal fat around the organs. It's an approved drug for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. That visceral-fat evidence is what sets it apart from everything else in this group.

items.d: Visceral-fat-targeted GHRH paired with the cleanest GHRP. A popular body-recomposition combination.
items.x: Combines the only secretagogue with real visceral-fat data with the cleanest GHRP. Popular for body recomposition where abdominal fat is the target. Expect a slow timeline — this is a months-long protocol, not a quick change.

items.d: Triple monoamine reuptake inhibitor used for strong appetite suppression. Not a GLP-1.
items.x: Blocks reuptake of all three major monoamines, producing appetite suppression through the brain rather than the gut. It reached phase III trials for obesity with solid weight loss results. It is not a GLP-1 and doesn't behave like one — the side effect profile is stimulant-shaped.

items.d: Bioregulator sold for testicular support, though there is almost no published research behind that use.
items.x: Sold as a testicular bioregulator, but there is essentially no research behind that use. The only primary experiment on the molecule involved binding to wheat proteins, and the citations in its own supporting review don't test it on reproductive tissue. The weakest-evidenced compound in this catalog.

items.d: Thymic dipeptide. An immune regulator, and a registered prescription drug in Russia at microgram doses.
items.x: A two-amino-acid thymic peptide, registered as a prescription immunomodulator in Russia for infections with weakened immunity. The approved dose is 100 micrograms — worth knowing, because vials sold here are typically 10mg, a hundred times that. Its anti-aging claim rests on a single rat study.

items.d: Thymic peptide that matures and directs T-cells. Immune restoration rather than blanket stimulation.
items.x: A thymic peptide that helps T-cells mature and directs the immune response rather than simply ramping it up. It's an approved drug in several countries for hepatitis B and as a vaccine adjuvant, and saw heavy use during COVID. The best-evidenced immune peptide in this list.

items.d: BPC-157 in a topical form applied directly over the injured area.
items.x: BPC-157 formulated for topical application directly over the injured area. Appealing for people avoiding injections, though how much peptide of this size actually crosses skin is an open question. Reasonable for superficial tissue, less convincing for a deep tendon.

items.d: Blood vessel bioregulator peptide. Endothelial function.
items.x: A bioregulator peptide directed at blood vessel lining. The vascular evidence is a single cell-culture study; its strongest data is actually neurological, from an Alzheimer's mouse model. Sold for one thing, evidenced for another.

items.d: Thymus bioregulator dipeptide. Immune support and gene reactivation in aged cells.
items.x: A thymus-derived dipeptide from the Russian bioregulator research programme. Cell studies show it loosening tightly-packed DNA in immune cells from elderly donors, reactivating dormant genes. Worth knowing the same study found a near-doubling of a DNA damage marker, which the authors read as activation and toxicologists would read differently.

items.d: Vasoactive intestinal peptide. Used for gut inflammation, immune balance and mould illness protocols.
items.x: A signalling peptide found throughout the gut and lungs with broad anti-inflammatory and immune-balancing effects. Most commonly used intranasally in mould illness and chronic inflammatory response protocols. Human evidence outside those niches is limited.

items.d: Injectable B12 for energy metabolism, red blood cell production and nerve health.
items.x: Injectable B12 for energy metabolism, red blood cell production and nerve health. The injection bypasses absorption issues common with age, vegan diets, metformin and acid-reducing medication. Deficiency is worth testing for rather than assuming.

items.d: Myostatin-inhibiting steroidal SARM hybrid. Potent, with liver toxicity potential.
items.x: Part SARM, part steroid, and reported to inhibit myostatin by raising follistatin. That myostatin angle is the appeal. It's structurally a steroid despite the SARM label, carries real hepatotoxicity potential, and has essentially no human data.
